deep.reconstruction:
CONTEXT. Opera Postuma (1862), Arithmetica, 'Fragmenta ex Adversariis depromta', p. 235. Two fragments appear here: the end of no. 5 (headed 'Lexell' on the previous page) and the start of no. 6.

FRAGMENT 5 (reduction of FLT; Lexell).
(1) Suppose c^λ = a^λ + b^λ. Then c^{2λ} − 4a^λb^λ = (a^λ+b^λ)^2 − 4a^λb^λ = (a^λ − b^λ)^2, which is a square.
(2) Put d = ab. Then c^{2λ} − 4d^λ would have to be a square. So FLT for exponent λ would follow from showing that c^{2λ} − 4d^λ = □ is impossible (in the relevant nontrivial sense), excepting λ = 1, 2.
(3) Corollary. In the same way b^λ = c^λ − a^λ gives b^{2λ} + 4c^λa^λ = (c^λ+a^λ)^2. Likewise a^{2λ} + 4c^λb^λ = (c^λ+b^λ)^2. These forms must therefore also be impossible.
(4) Attempt for λ = 3.
- Write a^3 + b^3 = c^3 as (a+b)(a^2−ab+b^2) = c^3.
- Treat the factors as coprime. The text dismisses the case gcd = 3 as raising 'no new difficulty'.
- Set a+b = p^3 and a^2−ab+b^2 = P^3, so c = Pp. Then p^6 − P^3 = (a+b)^2 − (a^2−ab+b^2) = 3ab.
- Similarly b^3 = (c−a)(c^2+ca+a^2). Set c−a = q^3 and c^2+ca+a^2 = Q^3, so b = Qq and Q^3 − q^6 = 3ac.
- Similarly a^3 = (c−b)(c^2+cb+b^2). Set c−b = r^3 and c^2+cb+b^2 = R^3, so a = Rr and R^3 − r^6 = 3bc.
(5) Substituting c = Pp, b = Qq, a = Rr gives the system:
- I: p^3 = Rr + Qq. II: q^3 = Pp − Rr. III: r^3 = Pp − Qq.
- IV: P^3 = R^2r^2 − RrQq + Q^2q^2. V: Q^3 = P^2p^2 + PpRr + R^2r^2. VI: R^3 = P^2p^2 + PpQq + Q^2q^2.
- VII: p^6 − P^3 = 3QqRr. VIII: Q^3 − q^6 = 3PpRr. IX: R^3 − r^6 = 3PpQq.
- Also Q^3 − P^3 = (c^2+ac+a^2) − (a^2−ab+b^2) = c^2 + ac + ab − b^2. This factors as (c+b)(a+c−b) = (Pp+Qq)(Rr+Pp−Qq).
The fragment ends with the goal of finding a contradiction in these conditions; none is derived.

FRAGMENT 6 (conjecture).
- Claim: there are no rationals A, B, C, ... whose sum times product equals 1. That is, AB(A+B) ≠ 1, ABC(A+B+C) ≠ 1, ABCD(A+B+C+D) ≠ 1, and so on.
- Equivalently, A+B+... ≠ 1/(AB...). Writing O = 1/(AB...), this reads: A+B+... ≠ O whenever AB...O = 1.
- Parametrize A = a/b, B = b/c, C = c/d, .... Then the product telescopes to a/(last), so O = (last)/a. The forbidden relations become a/b + b/c ≠ c/a, a/b + b/c + c/d ≠ d/a, etc.
- Announced consequence (proved on the next page): Theorem I, p^3 + q^3 ≠ r^3. [Mine: divide by pqr and set A = p^2/(qr), B = q^2/(pr), O = r^2/(pq); then ABO = 1.]
- On p. 236 the same device yields the general claim that n−1 n-th powers never sum to an n-th power. This is Euler's sum-of-powers conjecture.
- Fragment 7 (p. 236) then refutes the auxiliary conjecture with 4/3, 3/2, −1/3, −3/2, whose sum and product both equal 1.
errors: Slip in the last identity: the page (image too) has Q^3 − P^3 = (c−b)(a+c−b). The correct factorization is (c+b)(a+c−b), since Q^3 − P^3 = c^2 + ac + ab − b^2. The second form given, (Pp+Qq)(Rr+Pp−Qq), does equal (c+b)(a+c−b), so the slip is confined to the middle expression.

Unjustified dismissal of the gcd-3 case. Cubes mod 9 are 0, ±1, so in any primitive solution of a^3+b^3=c^3 exactly one of a, b, c is divisible by 3. Hence the three factorizations can never all have coprime factors. The system I–IX describes an empty situation for an elementary reason (mod 9), and the case set aside is in fact the only case. This is the classical 'second case' and the real difficulty.
Fragment 5 gives only a reduction (FLT_λ would follow from impossibility of c^{2λ} − 4d^λ = □). No proof is given, and the λ = 3 attempt stops without a contradiction.

Fragment 6's 'theorema demonstrandum' is false in general. A 4-term counterexample appears on the next page: (4/3)(3/2)(−1/3)(−3/2) = 1 and 4/3 + 3/2 − 1/3 − 3/2 = 1. The 2-term case AB(A+B) = 1 is true; it is equivalent to FLT for n = 3, via uv(u+v) = w^3.

Only the implication 'power relation ⇒ A+B+...=O with AB...O=1' holds, not the converse. The refutation of the auxiliary conjecture therefore does not by itself refute the derived 'theorems'. Those were later shown false directly: Lander–Parkin 1966 for n = 5, Elkies 1988 for n = 4.

results.what: Reduction: a^λ+b^λ=c^λ implies c^{2λ}−4(ab)^λ is a square, and also b^{2λ}+4(ac)^λ and a^{2λ}+4(bc)^λ are squares
results.modern_name: Elementary reduction of Fermat's equation to a quartic/sextic square condition (cf. the Frey-type quantity (a^λ−b^λ)^2 = c^{2λ}−4(ab)^λ)
results.usually_credited_to: Folklore; attributed in the fragment to Lexell / Euler

results.what: Triple factorization of a^3+b^3=c^3 into cubes (a+b=p^3, c−a=q^3, c−b=r^3, etc.) in the coprime case
results.modern_name: Standard first-case factorization for FLT n=3 (Abel/Barlow-type relations)
results.usually_credited_to: Barlow (1810), Abel (1823) for the general-n analogues

results.what: Conjecture that rationals cannot have (sum)(product)=1, used to 'derive' that n−1 n-th powers cannot sum to an n-th power
results.modern_name: Euler's sum of powers conjecture (via the device A=p^{n−1}/(qr...)...); the auxiliary equation is the 'sum times product = 1' Diophantine problem
results.usually_credited_to: Euler (conjecture, c. 1769); disproved by Lander–Parkin 1966 (n=5) and Elkies 1988 (n=4)

deep.surprise_reason: Euler's sum-of-powers conjecture is well known as his. This published Opera Postuma fragment shows a heuristic route to it through the false 'sum×product≠1' conjecture, which is refuted on the very next page. The Lexell reduction and the cube factorizations are routine. The detail is of mild historical interest but not new.

checkable.asserts: Cubes mod 9 are 0,±1, so one of a,b,c must be divisible by 3 (coprime case is empty)
Elkies' counterexample to Theorem II / Euler's conjecture for n=4
Lander–Parkin counterexample to Theorem III for n=5
ABO=1 for the substitution used in Theorem I

transcription_corrections: The impossibility sign is printed as a special crossed/bracketed equals symbol (resembling ⊐⊏), defined in the text; '≠' is an acceptable rendering.
The line 'Q^3−P^3=(c−b)(a+c−b)=(Pp+Qq)(Rr+Pp−Qq)' matches the image. The error (c−b) for (c+b) is in the source, not the transcription.
The fragment heading on the previous page is '5. (Lexell.)', and the closing reference on this page is 'p. 113.'; both are consistent with the image.
